overview: Democrats won the House in Tuesday's midterms, and several outlets report Republicans also lost the Senate, with a Mississippi Senate race still uncounted. A sharp tech sell-off pushed the Nasdaq into a correction, which outlets linked to investor worries about AI after the election. Abroad, hoax bomb threats disrupted dozens of European flights, Paraguay's president resigned after a digital bank collapse, and Israel's president will name who forms the next government on Sunday. In New York, six people died in a Sunset Park house fire where a lithium battery was found.

markets.summary: US tech stocks fell sharply on Thursday and the Nasdaq closed in correction territory, meaning it is more than 10% below a recent high. The Wall Street Journal called it the market's worst day since last April's tariff turmoil, and outlets tied it to fears that a Democratic Congress and states could crack down on AI and data centers. The selling spread to Asian chip and tech shares on Friday, though Nasdaq futures pointed higher in the morning. Oil slipped below $100 a barrel on hopes of a diplomatic end to the Iran war. The Bank of England raised rates and the Fed is widely expected to do the same in December, per the NYT; the US October jobs report is due Friday. Note that some index figures in the quote table are as of different dates.

concept.explanation: A correction is a drop of 10% or more in a stock index from its recent peak, short of the 20% fall usually called a bear market. Corrections are driven by shifts in expectations, such as worries about a hot sector, rising interest rates or political change, and they are common even in healthy markets. For you, the main effect is on retirement and brokerage accounts that hold index funds; a correction on paper only becomes a loss if you sell, and many investors who keep contributing buy shares at lower prices.
